   The TAM, or “total addressable market,” of news publications globally is $125.7 billion , according to the World Association of News Publishers. If it were possible to buy a share of Market A.M. ’s future revenue then that’s the sort of statistic a smart investment banker might mention.

   A smart investor, on the other hand, would hang on to their wallet. There’s nothing inherently wrong with guesstimating economic opportunities, but the more prominent, inflated, or specific they are, the worse of a sign it can be.

   Take mattress-in-a-box company Casper , whose 2020 initial public offering prospectus cited a “ global sleep economy ” of $432 billion. The company initially wanted to sell stock at between $17 and $19 a share but ended up pricing the IPO at $12. Despite a pandemic-stimulus-fueled golden age for unprofitable companies, the stock had dropped to $3.55 the following year when an offer to take Casper private was accepted.

   The same go-go era saw a company make even Wall Street blush . WeWork will forever be remembered for inventing “ community-adjusted Ebitda ,” a profit measure that excluded many expenses.

   Less-remembered is its estimate of a $3 trillion TAM based on almost every office worker on Earth being a potential customer. The landlord portrayed itself as a tech company and snagged a private valuation of $47 billion. But its planned 2019 IPO had to be pulled. It filed for bankruptcy in 2023.

   For companies that eventually turned profitable, hyperbole can be forgiven as a youthful indiscretion. Airbnb had a TAM of $3.4 trillion and Uber $5.7 trillion for personal mobility alone. Leave it to Elon Musk, though, to say “hold my beer.” SpaceX, in documents for its June IPO, cited the “largest actionable” TAM “ in human history ” at a cool $28.5 trillion.

   In his post-IPO estimate of SpaceX’s value , New York University’s Aswath Damodaran wrote that “the estimation of TAM has been gamified by Silicon Valley, with bloated and patently unreachable numbers.”

   Another thing many TAM estimates have in common is that they’re oddly specific, often going out a decimal point. It’s probably no accident. In his book “ Proofiness ,” science writer Charles Seife calls it “disestimation,” getting us to ignore statistical uncertainty.

   Loss-making companies that go public have an especially patchy record, according to University of Florida professor Jay Ritter . They tend to do much better on the days of their IPOs than profitable ones. Individual investors rarely get to reap that gain, though. After that, the average return of the nearly 4,000 money-losing companies Ritter studied was negative 20.5% over three years relative to the market.

   Bankers often sell the sizzle, not the steak.

This newsletter’s readership is growing enough to keep your faithful writer employed—thank you—but why am I thinking so small?

 

The TAM, or “total addressable market,” of news publications globally is $125.7 billion, according to the World Association of News Publishers. If it were possible to buy a share of Market A.M.’s future revenue then that’s the sort of statistic a smart investment banker might mention.

 

A smart investor, on the other hand, would hang on to their wallet. There’s nothing inherently wrong with guesstimating economic opportunities, but the more prominent, inflated, or specific they are, the worse of a sign it can be.

 

Take mattress-in-a-box company Casper, whose 2020 initial public offering prospectus cited a “global sleep economy” of $432 billion. The company initially wanted to sell stock at between $17 and $19 a share but ended up pricing the IPO at $12. Despite a pandemic-stimulus-fueled golden age for unprofitable companies, the stock had dropped to $3.55 the following year when an offer to take Casper private was accepted.

 

The same go-go era saw a company make even Wall Street blush. WeWork will forever be remembered for inventing “community-adjusted Ebitda,” a profit measure that excluded many expenses.

 

Less-remembered is its estimate of a $3 trillion TAM based on almost every office worker on Earth being a potential customer. The landlord portrayed itself as a tech company and snagged a private valuation of $47 billion. But its planned 2019 IPO had to be pulled. It filed for bankruptcy in 2023.

 

For companies that eventually turned profitable, hyperbole can be forgiven as a youthful indiscretion. Airbnb had a TAM of $3.4 trillion and Uber $5.7 trillion for personal mobility alone. Leave it to Elon Musk, though, to say “hold my beer.” SpaceX, in documents for its June IPO, cited the “largest actionable” TAM “in human history” at a cool $28.5 trillion.

 

In his post-IPO estimate of SpaceX’s value, New York University’s Aswath Damodaran wrote that “the estimation of TAM has been gamified by Silicon Valley, with bloated and patently unreachable numbers.”

 

Another thing many TAM estimates have in common is that they’re oddly specific, often going out a decimal point. It’s probably no accident. In his book “Proofiness,” science writer Charles Seife calls it “disestimation,” getting us to ignore statistical uncertainty.

 

Loss-making companies that go public have an especially patchy record, according to University of Florida professor Jay Ritter. They tend to do much better on the days of their IPOs than profitable ones. Individual investors rarely get to reap that gain, though. After that, the average return of the nearly 4,000 money-losing companies Ritter studied was negative 20.5% over three years relative to the market.

 

Bankers often sell the sizzle, not the steak.
